videos.title: 美光暴涨！AI能够改变“周期”规律吗？ | Micron | MU | 镁光 | 半导体 | HBM | 高带宽内存 |  三星 |  海力士
videos.transcript: Micron released an earnings report so  incredible it’s hard to believe: Q1  revenue hit $ 5.42 billion, with $  13.32 billion for the full year—more  than triple the previous year's $ 3.74  billion—and the company expects to  set new records next quarter. It sounds  like a high-growth tech company, but  historically, Micron has always been  considered a cyclical stock. So the  question is: has AI truly made the  cycle obsolete? Or have we once again  fallen for the most expensive phrase in  investing? "This time is different." In  this video, I want to use Micron's  earnings report to talk about what I  believe is the most important and  unavoidable topic in investing: the  cycle. Hi everyone, this is US Stock  Doctor, sharing insights on US stocks  every week. For today's video, make  sure to watch until the end. In the  first part of the video, let's discuss  why Micron is performing so strongly  this round. If you are already very  familiar with what Micron does, feel  free to skip to this timestamp. Micron  mainly produces memory: the chips  responsible for storing data in  computers, smartphones, and servers.  This is mainly divided into two  categories: DRAM, which is memory used  for temporary data during operations,  and NAND, which is flash storage used  for files in phones and hard drives.  Historically, the two types of products  produced by memory manufacturers have  had two distinct characteristics. First , commoditization. For example, when we  buy a laptop, we only look at the  capacity of the memory and hard drive.  As for who manufactures them, the vast  majority of people couldn't care less.  Because these products are essentially  standardized, they are interchangeable  between manufacturers, meaning there is  severe commoditization. When products  are severely commoditized, it is  difficult to rely on brand pricing.  Second is the marginal effect. Since  the costs of factory equipment and  production lines are mostly fixed, the  marginal cost of producing memory  sticks is relatively low. This is a bit  like oil companies, where equipment  costs are high, but once the process is  running, production scales easily.  Producing less just means earning less,  while producing more means earning more ; as long as memory prices rise  slightly, the extra revenue almost  entirely becomes profit. Due to the  commoditization of products and low  marginal costs, the storage industry  has been trapped in a profit cycle for  decades. Prices mainly depend on supply  and demand: when demand is strong,  prices rise, leading manufacturers to  expand capacity. As supply increases,  prices fall, profits shrink, and  manufacturers cut investment, causing  supply to contract. This eventually  weeds out poorly managed companies  before the next cycle begins. This  makes these companies money-printing  machines during upturns and meat  grinders during downturns, reflecting  highly distinct cyclical  characteristics. Therefore, the capital  market typically gives these highly  cyclical companies low valuations,  usually around 10 times. So, why do  these storage manufacturers seem to  have broken out of the cycle this time?  We all know the answer. That answer is  AI. AI has driven demand toward HBM and  high-performance memory. As prices have  risen and operating leverage has been  magnified, profits have exploded. Many  people might ask: since we all consider  these cyclical stocks that earn  cyclical profits, why does this stock  price surge make so many people feel  that this cycle is different from the  past? I have summarized the answer in  three points. First, industry  expectations show that the share of HBM  and server DRAM in AI servers is rising  rapidly, and the share of memory in AI  infrastructure spending is also  expanding. This is not just a simple  replacement cycle, but a continuous  infrastructure build-out. Second,  top-tier customers have locked in  capacity through strategic agreements  by paying prepayments or deposits.  Taking Micron as an example, the  proportion of such agreements extending  to 2030 and 2031 has increased  significantly, with a massive scale of  remaining performance obligations.  Third, while these companies mainly  produced highly commoditized memory and  hard drives in the past, the product  characteristics of AI-related offerings  have led to shifts in their business  models. First, the technical  architecture differences are  significant, increasing manufacturing  complexity and entry barriers. Second,  customer customization raises the entry  threshold, as these major customers all  sign long-term supply agreements. All  of these factors have weakened the  cyclical nature of these storage stocks . However, we still need to clearly  distinguish two things: AI requires  more HBM, a fact visible in financial  reports. How long this demand will last  and how large it will be depends not  only on the judgment of Micron's  management but also on market  expectations, which is to say, investor  sentiment. Micron emphasizes that AI is  driving the entire storage ecosystem of  HBM, DRAM, and SSDs. However, this is  the company's own assessment of the  industry; we can use it as a reference,  but we must never treat it as an  objective fact. So, regarding storage  stocks, is this truly a brand-new  growth story, or just another very  strong cyclical story? Next, we will  enter the second part: why is money in  cyclical stocks so hard to make? Former  Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan  once said, "We only know it's a bubble  when it bursts." Cycles have a similar  concept: the last day of a bull market  is the beginning of a bear market, and  the last day of a bear market happens  to be the start of a bull market. The  strangest thing about a cycle is that  it never tells you when the top is. On  the contrary, it presents a mountain of  data to show us how good things are  this time: great orders, great prices,  great profits, confident management,  and analysts constantly raising  expectations. For example, take a  cyclical stock: profit of 1 billion in  year one, 2 billion in year two, 4  billion in year three, and 8 billion in  year four. Seeing profits double  continuously, we start to feel that  this company's growth potential is  outstanding. But the real question is:  is this 8 billion the normal profit it  can earn in the future, or is it the  profit at the peak of the cycle? This  question is almost impossible to answer  objectively during an upturn, because  all signals reinforce the same judgment . We begin to believe that past  patterns might not apply this time, and  this is what Howard Marks repeatedly  warns us about: "This time is different ." As the co-founder of Oaktree Capital , his memos, updated periodically on  their website, are required reading  that Buffett has always recommended to  us ordinary investors. In his discourse  on cycles, he has emphasized more than  once that when a cycle begins or ends  is basically impossible to predict, but  we can strive to judge another fact:  roughly where we are in the cycle.  Predicting the future asks us to name  the "peak" date, while judging our  position involves looking at current  prices, sentiment, supply, and  investment behavior—whether people  are pessimistic or optimistic, whether  no one dares to expand production or  everyone is rushing to do so. To  clarify, Howard Marks is talking about  general cycles and human behavior, not  making a specific judgment on Micron,  right? It's not that anyone who says " this time is different" is necessarily  wrong. Sometimes it really is different , just like the internet or smartphones , which truly changed their industries.  But the real question is what exactly  is different: has the demand structure  changed, has the supply structure  shifted, has the competitive landscape  evolved, has the pace of capital  expenditure changed, or is it simply  that investors are more optimistic than  before? The former points are real  changes, while the last one is merely  sentiment. The danger lies in jumping  directly from "this time is truly  different" to "all past rules no longer  apply"—there is a vast gap between  those two statements. Returning to  Micron, the market has reason to  believe this time is different because  AI demand is clearly structural. HBM  has higher barriers, tighter  integration with advanced packaging and  GPUs, and AI customers prioritize  supply, willing to lock in capacity  with long-term contracts, while new  capacity takes longer to build. Each of  these factors could make the cycle  longer and stronger, but a longer cycle  and the disappearance of the cycle are  two different things. Since the cycle  hasn't disappeared, let's move on to  the third part: how should we actually  view AI's impact on the cycle? Let me  share my judgment first—note that  this is my analysis, not a proven fact.  AI may have changed the shape of the  cycle, but it certainly will not make  the cycle disappear. I think we should  focus not on how much money Micron is  making, but on what changes have  actually occurred in the industry's  supply and demand. As mentioned in the  first part, profit is just a result.  Regarding supply and demand, to  understand AI's impact on this memory  cycle, we need to look at three levels:  supply, demand, and pricing. The first  layer is demand, which determines how  far the cycle can go. In the past,  memory relied mainly on PCs and  smartphones, with limited market growth . Now, with AI data centers added,  we've moved from a mobile-driven cycle  to one that now includes AI  infrastructure. So we must look at two  things: first, AI capital expenditure —are major clients like Nvidia,  Amazon, Google, and Meta continuing to  increase their investment? If demand is  strong, but the support for that demand  appears to be slowing significantly, we  must re-evaluate. The second is whether  HBM demand itself remains strong, and  how the pricing, capacity, and customer  certification are holding up.  Especially with HBM4, the next  generation of technological upgrades  could either solidify barriers or  reshuffle the industry. Second is the  discussion of supply, which determines  when the cycle will turn. If demand  doubles and supply also doubles, prices  may not necessarily rise. The  characteristic of memory is that supply  is slow; you have to build plants, buy  equipment, adjust processes, improve  yields, and pass customer  certifications. Thus, demand shifts,  supply lags, leading to price hikes and  explosive profits. This is the current  situation. So, when will supply catch  up? It depends on two things. First is  capital expenditure, as today's capital  expenditure determines future supply.  Therefore, to judge if industry profits  are high, we can't just look at how  much a company earns; we must ask if  the industry is expanding capacity  frantically. If everyone believes  prices will remain high for years, they  will invest aggressively, which may set  the stage for the next phase. However,  it must be clear that increased capital  expenditure does not equal an immediate  bottom; it only indicates that future  supply is growing. Second is the  timeline for new capacity to come  online. We cannot just look at  investment announcements, but must see  when facilities are built, production  scales up, and effective supply is  truly formed. Announcements and actual  supply are two different things. Third  is price; price is the most honest  signal, telling us whether changes have  truly occurred. First, we need to  monitor: are the prices of DRAM and  NAND still rising? Has the pace of  growth slowed down? Is customer  inventory healthy? If inventory begins  to pile up, it indicates that supply is  starting to change. Second is long-term  agreements. Micron emphasizes that  strategic customer agreements provide  better future revenue visibility, which  is good, but improved visibility  doesn't mean the cycle has disappeared;  agreements lock in volume and price for  a period, not the industry-wide supply  and demand. Thus, demand determines how  far the cycle goes, supply determines  when the cycle shifts, and price  determines whether the change has truly  happened—these three are intertwined.  Seeing this, I believe many may feel  I've made things more confusing,  leaving you unsure whether to invest in  storage companies like Micron. I think  my purpose has been achieved, because  this video isn't meant to tell you if  you should buy Micron or not, but to  share where the real difficulty in  investing in these stocks lies. If you  don't have a deep understanding of the  demand, supply, and price factors I  mentioned, then your purchase of these  stocks is very likely blind, or will at  least significantly increase your  chance of losing money. If you aren't  absolutely certain, you might want to  do as I do and stay away from these  highly cyclical storage stocks. Of  course, I am not denying in this video  that AI has brought structural changes  in demand to the storage industry.  HBM's technical barriers are indeed  higher, supply improvements are more  difficult, and wealthy major clients  are willing to pay more to maintain  supply stability. These factors have  significantly extended this cycle, but  as long as there is supply, capital  expenditure, and price competition, the  cycle can never be completely  eliminated. It may become longer, more  complex, and fluctuate in ways  different from what we previously  understood, but the cycle itself still  exists. So when a company delivers its  most dazzling financial results in  history, we shouldn't just look at how  much higher it can go; we should focus  on whether its current profit is the  company's long-term capability or just  a gift from the cycle in the short term . The hardest part of investing has  never been understanding current  financial reports, but rather, once  financial reports are compounded by  industry cycles and macroeconomics, it  becomes difficult to judge the  company's true current state. I have  always believed that the most expensive  words in investing are "this time is  different." So, for Micron and even the  storage industry, is it truly " different this time," or have we once  again fallen for "this time is  different"? I welcome you all to share  your thoughts with me in the comments  section. Alright, that is the cycle I  wanted to discuss with everyone using  Micron's latest financial report as a  basis. Next, let's move on to the  portfolio disclosure. Hello, everyone.  The return for this week is 2.23%.  Since March 2022, the total account  return is 252.17%. There is only the  weekly $ 100 investment in Microsoft,  with no other changes. This week, I  want to talk about Eli Lilly. At the  recently concluded EASD 2024, Eli Lilly  announced the phase 2b data for its  latest multi-target combination weight  loss regimen. Let me first clarify what  this multi-target combination regimen  is: it is not a single triple-target  molecule, but rather Lilly combining  its existing dual-target weight loss  drug tirzepatide with a single-target  drug, orforglipron, to act on three  targets simultaneously. Lilly hopes to  push weight loss results even further  by layering different mechanisms. This  phase 2b trial enrolled 700 patients  who were obese or overweight and also  had type 2 diabetes, with a treatment  duration of 48 weeks, and the results  were indeed very impressive. In the  highest dose group, which was 9mg of  orforglipron plus the current highest  dose of 15mg of tirzepatide, the  average weight loss reached 23.3%. For  comparison, using 15mg of tirzepatide  alone for 48 weeks resulted in an  average weight loss of 14.8%. In other  words, in this experiment, adding  orforglipron increased weight loss by  8.5%. Regarding blood sugar, HbA1c in  the highest dose group decreased by 2.9 %, while tirzepatide alone decreased it  by 2.4%. However, there is a question  here that is very worth noting for  investors: if the effect is  significantly stronger, what is the  cost? The answer is gastrointestinal  side effects and the discontinuation  rate. The most common adverse reactions  in the trials remain gastrointestinal  issues such as nausea, diarrhea,  constipation, and vomiting, most of  which occur during the dose-escalation  phase. What is worth noting here is  that adverse events are more common in  the combination therapy group, with the  high-dose multi-target combination  group reporting an adverse event rate  as high as 27%, compared to only 2.9%in  the Retatrutide group. In other words,  the key issue with this drug is not  whether it can help lose more weight,  but whether it can help more patients  stick with the treatment, which is  precisely why Eli Lilly is the company  most worth watching right now. 估值的消化，最典型的就是此前存储股所经历的大规模下跌。那这是好公司被便宜的卖掉，因为热钱暂时流走了，但基本面恶化是完全不同的情况，它是公司本身出了问题，前者是机会，后者是陷阱。所以相信很多朋友们现在手里有大量的AI股票，我们一定要区分手中的这些股票。 到底，他们现在是已经有了明显的基本面改善，还是依然处在一个炒概念的阶段？ 这将决定当这样的市场冲击来临时，他们能否经得起考验。总而言之，说了这么多数据来给朋友们说些干货，现在到底应该怎么操作？第一，我认为一定要做的就是我们的核心仓位，千万不要动。 但这个大前提是一定要，确保我们手中的股票是高质量，已经有稳定的现金流和健康的财务报表，并且估值也处在一个相对合理的水平的股票。 那注意我们要做的是部分的止盈，而不是清仓。这是为了让我们手中留有部分的现金，一旦出现机会时，我们还有钱能够补进去。但如果没有出现大幅度的下跌，我们也不会完全的踏空。 第三点就是我们把购物清单写出来，提前确定下来我们想要抄底的股票，并且写上明显的价位。那这一点现在听起来或许非常简单，因为我们心情是非常平静的，可以理性的判断哪些公司值得买买在什么位置。但当市场出现大规模回调的时候。 第四点，我们要做的就是留现金，并且不要用过度的杠杆，无论是快速的涨还是跌，在一个我们已经明知道波动会放大的窗口里加杠杆是最没有必要的风险现金在这种时候。 不是闲置，它反而是一个期权。如果风险没有发生，我们本来就有仓位在市场里，但如果风险发生了，现金就是全场最值钱的东西。那现在市场的机会到底在哪里？ If the threat is cheap and your interceptor is exquisite, you win the shot and lose the war of attrition. Legacy missiles are fixed architectures. Years to redesign, hard to scale. Over a sustained fight that is punishing. Steelfin is Anderil's answer. a family of surfaceto-air interceptors built around a common two-stage architecture. Stage one, a booster you can swap. Stage two, a terminal interceptor that shares the same baseline airframe, avionics, and software. Modular means different rocket motors, different seekers, different launchers. Reconfigure, don't redesign. From cheap drones up through crews, ballistic, and hypersonic threats. Company target per breaking defense about one-third a PAC3 MSE. Andreil has not published a firm unit price. Production intent several thousand a year short-term. Flight tests next year. The way I see it, the product isn't one missile. It's an architecture that matches cost to the threat. So, is 1/3 of a pack 3 the right bet on mass defense or still too expensive for cheap drones?
